summary.title: An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units
summary.one_liner: Learn how the IBM System/360 Model 91 floating-point unit used a common data bus and register tagging to run independent instructions in parallel without specially optimized code.
keywords: how does out-of-order cpu execution work
takeaways: A simple common data bus plus register tagging lets independent instructions execute simultaneously while preserving data dependencies.
The hardware looks ahead about eight instructions to optimize execution locally, without requiring specially optimized code.
The same techniques apply to almost any computer with multiple execution units and one or more accumulators, not only floating-point or System/360.
This paper is the origin of tag-based renaming and reservation stations that underlie modern out-of-order issue queues.
summary.summary: This IBM paper describes the floating-point design of the System/360 Model 91 for exploiting multiple execution units. Its core mechanisms are a simple common data bus and register tagging scheme, which allow independent instructions to run concurrently while keeping the necessary ordering between dependent ones. The hardware achieves this by looking ahead roughly eight instructions. The abstract notes the approach generalizes to other machines with multiple execution units and accumulators, and that the execution units, buffers and I/O buses are extensively checked. The listing describes it as the origin of tag-based renaming and reservation stations.
